title: Post stitches (FPDC and BPDC)
subtitle: Wrapping the hook around the post for deep ribbing and cable effects
excerpt: Post stitches insert the hook around the vertical post of the stitch below rather than into the top loops. Front post (FPDC) pulls the stitch toward you; back post (BPDC) pushes it away. Alternating them creates the deepest crochet ribbing and the basis for crochet cables.
sourceNotes: Post stitch technique synthesised from standard crochet teaching. FPDC and BPDC are modern technique names; the underlying method of working around the post of the stitch is referenced in Weldon's Practical Crochet for raised-texture work (Internet Archive).
heroPrompt: A swatch of FPDC/BPDC ribbing in DK cotton, showing the deep textured rib formed by front and back post stitches alternating, cream yarn on natural linen background.

glossaryTerms.definition: A double crochet worked around the vertical post of the stitch below by inserting the hook from front to back to front (going around the post). The stitch body pushes forward toward the viewer.
A double crochet worked around the vertical post by inserting the hook from back to front to back. The stitch body sits away from the viewer, creating a recessed column.

content.text: Standard stitches work into the top loops. Post stitches go around the outside of the stitch post — the vertical column of yarn that holds the stitch upright. Working around the post instead of into the top moves the stitch body forward or backward against the fabric plane, which is what creates the dimensional rib texture.
Front post double crochet (FPDC)
Identify the next stitch in the row below (the stitch that will become the post to work around).
Insert the hook from FRONT to back, going around the right side of the post.
Bring the hook around the back of the post and return to the front on the left side of the post.
The hook is now wrapped around the post with two loops on the hook (the loop it carried plus the one pulled around). Yarn over and pull through both loops. The front post dc is complete.
Back post double crochet (BPDC)
Insert the hook from BACK to front, going around the right side of the post from behind.
Bring the hook around the front of the post and return to the back on the left side.
Yarn over and pull through both loops.

attrs.title: Post stitches need a foundation row
attrs.body: Post stitches cannot be worked into a chain or a very thin stitch — the post needs to be tall enough to wrap around. Work a foundation row of standard double crochet or treble first. Post stitches always work into the row BELOW the current row, not the row immediately behind the hook.

content.text: FPDC/BPDC ribbing pattern
Foundation: ch 18. Row 1: dc in 2nd ch from hook and in each chain across (17 dc). Turn.
Row 2 (rib row): ch 1, *FPDC around next st, BPDC around next st; repeat from * across, dc in last st. Turn.
Row 3: ch 1, *FPDC around the FPDC stitch, BPDC around the BPDC stitch; repeat from * across, dc in last st. Turn.
Repeat row 3. Work the post stitch around the post of the SAME type of post stitch from the row before — FP on FP, BP on BP.
Front post treble (FPTR) and back post treble (BPTR)

Post stitches can be any height. Front post treble (FPTR) and back post treble (BPTR) work the same way as FPDC/BPDC but with a treble (one yarn over before inserting). Taller post stitches create a more pronounced, cord-like rib and are the basis for crochet cables: arrange FPTR in groups and cross them (like the crossed treble technique but worked around posts) to make cable-look panels.
Common mistakes

items.symptom: The post stitch is very tight and the hook barely fits around the post
items.cause: The foundation stitches were worked at a tight tension.
items.fix: Work the foundation row looser than normal. Post stitches need room to wrap around; tight posts refuse the hook.

items.symptom: The ribbing goes flat instead of being dimensional
items.cause: Working FPDC instead of BPDC on the alternating stitches (or vice versa), so both post stitches push the same direction.
items.fix: On each rib row, work FPDC on the raised (FP) columns and BPDC on the recessed (BP) columns. The pattern creates the push-pull that makes the rib dimensional.

items.symptom: The stitch count grows with every post stitch row
items.cause: Working the post stitch AND an additional stitch into the same position.
items.fix: A post stitch replaces the top-loop stitch at that position. Do not add a separate stitch above the post stitch as well.

content.text: What to try next

Crochet cables use FPTR crossed over each other (like the crossed treble technique but with post trebles) to make cable-panel patterns. A simple 4-stitch cable: work 2 BPTR, then cross 2 FPTR over each other (right over left for a right-leaning cable). The post stitches tutorial in this library has the full cable method.
